title: A bot that wins 90% of its trades can still lose money. It's not always about the win-rate...
author: LuckOrEdge
selftext:
Socila media accounts love to show a high win rate and some people online are obsessed with this metric.   
  
Take a bot that wins 90% of its trades. Each win makes +1R. Each loss costs −12R. Bots that take small profits and let losers run, like some grid and averaging-down bots, can look exactly like this.  
  
Over 100 trades:  
  
\- 90 wins × +1R = +90R  
\- 10 losses × −12R = −120R  
\- Net: −30R, or −0.3R per trade  
  
To break even, this bot needs 12 ÷ 13 = 92.3% winners. A 90% win rate sounds great but would still lose in this situation.   
  
Why bots like this look so good at first:  
  
\- A 10-trade demo shows zero losses about 35% of the time.  
\- I simulated 100,000 runs of 100 trades each. Only 21% finished in profit.  
  
The most importan questions to ask about any bot or AI strategy before trusting its win rate:  
  
1. How big is the average loss compared with the average win?  
2. How many trades is the record based on? A few dozen trades can't differentiate edge from luck.  
3. What was the worst drawdown and how likely will it happen again?  
  
Is anyone using a strategy with a high win-rate that has a proper risk to reward ratio?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the 10-trade demo stat is the scary one. a grid bot can go months without meeting its -12R day, so the record looks spotless right up until it doesn't.

I built Quantradin to run rules like that on practice money against real prices first, and its card draws the whole equity curve, so a -12R day shows up as a cliff instead of hiding inside a percentage. quantradin.com

in your 100k runs, how many trades did it usually take before the first big loss showed up?

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: In about 50% of the simulations, the -12R loss happened at the 7th trade and in 10% of the simulations it happened at the 22nd trade.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that's a sharper way to say it than mine. half the runs hit it by trade 7, so a 10-trade demo is close to a coin flip on ever showing the loss.

comments.author: Tradenoss
comments.body: good breakdown. one i'd add to the list: what the bot does with a losing trade when there's no stop. a lot of grid and averaging bots don't have one, so the -12R isn't a fixed number, it's whatever the market does that week

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: Good point. Without a fixed stop loss, your risk could (theoratically) be unlimited.

replies.author: DadsGamesandCharles
replies.body:
Only if you never made a kill switch or an override for yourself. All of us need that with our bots/algos. Completely taking the human out of the equation is one of the worst things you can do because then you can never stop a D-Day. You may NEVER need it and you may NEVER use it, but you should have it.

There are other ways to negate the no stop loss account killer; manual stops, hand trading the profit, 5% more SL than a median dip day on the stock, all sorts of ways, but just hitting stop or selling the stock that’s killing you  is the best way.

Don’t let drawdown stop your theory because in a real world you wouldn’t let it hurt you as bad as the backtest said you would. You just HAVE to know when you need to step in and when you just need to trust what you’ve built.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good example, and the break-even calculation is the number I'd want every bot post to show. One thing I'd add is that losses in these setups often come in a cluster, so the worst drawdown can be much bigger than the average loss suggests. Looking at it by trade count also helps, since a record of a few dozen trades says very little. If you want to test your own rule this way, Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and a held out stretch of data.

comments.author: DadsGamesandCharles
comments.body:
A proper risk to reward ratio is based on the user, not the algo or AI.

I say that because the user determines what the AI is going to use, in a normal world anyway, I see some of yall just saying, “Make me money,” and I’m like, wow.

100 trades is nothing, you need a lot more, like, a LOT. I wouldn’t even go into live testing without at least 1000 and I’d rather have 5000. There only way you’re not going to need more than that is if you’re only tracking like, 10 stocks total, then you might get the baseline.

To me, there is no proper risk to reward if you’re using AI unless you’re intimately familiar with the system and it’s been running a long time. Otherwise, it’s just guessing, it’ll end up being and looking like the same thing a human does when they move from paper to live money. 

Also, the best bots I’ve made have a low win rate with a crazy high ROI, win rate means a lot but it’s just a portion of the whole.

Great post.

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: Absolutely, 100 trades would most likely not be enough to get a statistical significant edge in the market. I also wouldn't deploy any bot with so few trades.
